analysis.one_liner: Restores a stiff estate tax on large inheritances and closes loopholes the wealthy use to avoid it.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and died with no cosponsors, so the 55% top estate-tax rate and anti-avoidance rules it proposed never took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have brought back a much larger estate tax: it cut the untaxed amount from $5 million to $1 million per estate, raised the top rate to 55% for estates over $10 million, and closed common loopholes — discounting family business assets, short-term 'GRAT' trusts, perpetual dynasty trusts, and reporting a low value to the IRS and a high value to the buyer of inherited assets. In the current system the first $5 million-plus of an estate passes tax-free and the top rate is 40%. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal government would have collected billions more from large inheritances, and the tax burden would have shifted onto the largest estates — those over $1 million, with the 55% rate applying above $10 million — while closing loopholes that let wealthy families pass assets nearly tax-free through generations. Ordinary taxpayers benefit from the resulting revenue, since the estate tax's proceeds offset taxes others must pay, and a fairer overall system. It also protected the tax base itself by requiring heirs to report inherited values consistent with what the estate reported.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday taxpayers and heirs outside the top 1%

how_it_helps.text: It lowers the estate-tax exclusion from $5 million to $1 million and raises top rates to 55%, so large inheritances would face tax that currently goes untaxed, producing revenue instead of a tax break for heirs.

It closes avoidance techniques used mainly by the rich: no valuation discounts for family business interests with inherited cash or passive assets stuffed in, no minority-interest discounts when the family keeps control, and minimum 10-year terms for grantor retained annuity trusts (a trust arrangement used to shift appreciated assets to heirs tax-free).
It ends the tax break that lets 'perpetual dynasty trusts' escape generation-skipping transfer tax forever: after 90 years, such trusts would owe the tax.

It requires that inherited property's tax basis match what the estate reported and that executors disclose the value of each interest to the IRS and to heirs, closing a gap where estates reported a low value for tax and heirs later claimed a high value to dodge capital-gains tax.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy families with estates over $1 million would pay higher estate taxes, and wealthy families and their advisers would lose access to the avoidance techniques (valuation discounts, GRATs, dynasty trusts, basis games) the bill targets. Estate-planning professionals would see reduced demand for those services.

drawbacks.text: The $1 million exclusion is far below the existing $5 million threshold, meaning the tax would reach many moderately well-off families — for example a family with a paid-off home, a small business, or farmland — not just the very wealthy, and the bill's rate table starts taxing at 41% on the first dollar over $1 million.

Executors and beneficiaries would face new reporting duties and penalties for filing inconsistent basis statements, adding paperwork and compliance costs to the process of settling an estate even before any tax is due.

Restricting minority-interest discounts and limiting GRAT terms could push wealthy families toward other, still-legal avoidance strategies, so the bill might raise less revenue than the rate schedule implies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had real anti-abuse teeth: closing valuation discounts, tightening GRATs, and requiring consistent basis reporting targeted estate-tax avoidance techniques that only the very wealthy can use. Its main drawbacks are design questions an honest supporter would acknowledge: the $1 million threshold is low and not indexed to the real cost of estates in high-cost areas until 2016 formulas kicked in, richer families and their advisers would have restructured around the rules, and the administrative burden of new disclosure rules would fall on executors and heirs of all kinds of estates. Weighed against that, the status quo lets the largest fortunes pass largely untaxed, so the cost of inaction falls on everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two entries: it was introduced on March 23, 2015, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had a single sponsor.
The Ways and Means Committee, which decides whether estate-tax legislation moves in the House, never considered it, and the bill never received a vote in either chamber.
Because the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without action, the bill expired; measures that die in committee must be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest families whose estates would have paid up to 55% in tax, and the estate-planning industry that helps them minimize it, were better off because the bill never advanced. Ordinary taxpayers continue to cover the revenue that a stronger estate tax would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy families and their estate planners

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 23, 2015 to raise estate-tax rates, lower the exclusion to $1 million, and close valuation and trust loopholes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so it never advanced.

against.name: Anti-tax advocacy groups and estate-tax opponents
against.role: Outside groups opposing the estate tax
against.what_they_did: Ran long-running campaigns against any expansion of the estate tax, keeping repeal a Republican priority and making committee action on an expansion politically unattractive.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only supporter was a single House Democrat with no cosponsors; with Republicans controlling the House and the Ways and Means Committee, no Republican backed it and the committee took no action.

industries.industry: Very wealthy households and large estates
industries.note: Estates over $1 million would pay up to 55% tax, and the bill targeted the valuation discounts, GRATs, and dynasty trusts their estate planners use to shrink the bill. For everyone else, this means large fortunes begin contributing revenue they currently avoid.

The bill's core provisions restrict the techniques (valuation discounts, GRAT planning, dynasty trusts, basis games) that generate much of high-end estate-planning work. Its death preserved that market.

The bill listed farmland and transfer taxes among its subjects and a lower $1 million threshold would reach some farm and small-business estates, though the valuation rules included a working-capital exception and a credit for state taxes paid (S3). Its death left their estates untaxed but also left everyone else covering the revenue.
